preamble: The deletion of the velar nasal /ŋ/ in word-initial position is a documented sound change across unrelated language families, driven by the cross-linguistic rarity and articulatory difficulty of word-initial /ŋ/ in many phonological systems. It is attested in ongoing change in Hong Kong Cantonese, where the onset /ŋ/ is merging with a zero onset, and as a completed change in dialects of Bininj Kunwok (Northern Australia). Initial-consonant loss is also a hallmark of several Pama-Nyungan subgroups in Australia, including Northern Paman (Uradhi ani < *nga:ni 'what') and Arandic (Arrernte aye- < *ngayu 'I'), and Arabana dropped /ŋ/- within the historical record.

examples.note: 我 'I/me'; word-initial /ŋ/ is deleted, merging with the zero-onset class. The change is widespread in younger speakers and is stigmatized by prescriptivists as 'lazy pronunciation' (懶音).
牛 'cow'; another high-frequency word where onset /ŋ/ is variably deleted.
Buffalo (loanword); word-initial /ŋ/ has been deleted in dialects of this non-Pama-Nyungan language of western Arnhem Land, Northern Territory, Australia.
The velar nasal initial of Middle Chinese is lost in Mandarin; Cantonese 我 ngo5 keeps it.
Compensatory lengthening; *ŋ was lost except before k.
The final nasal is lost and only nasalization of the vowel remains.
Initial *ŋ is lost in Northern Paman; Mpalitjanh, Yinwum, Linngithigh and Ngkoth also have ani. Kuuk Thaayorre nga:n keeps it.
Arandic lost initial consonants; Nhanda ngayi and Kalkatungu ngayi keep the nasal.
Kaytetye erlwe 'forehead' shows the same loss.
Initial /ŋ/ elision in Arabana continued into the 20th century.
